query: In conventional alloys, loss of toughness has long been associated with grain-boundary segregation and brittle grain-boundary precipitation. By contrast, compositionally complex high-entropy alloys can suppress rapid grain coarsening and deleterious intermetallic formation and have shown favorable strength–ductility combinations and resistance to high-temperature softening and low-temperature embrittlement. These findings do not establish what governs possible toughness degradation in an initially single-phase high-entropy alloy. Under the constraint of retaining a compositionally complex alloy suitable for demanding engineering service, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains whether and why brittle behavior emerges? Specify a controlled comparison that would distinguish the hypothesis from conventional-alloy expectations, predicted observations relative to the initial baseline, its service and loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification outcome.

generation.hypothesis: Tailoring the grain boundary morphology to achieve a serrated (undulated) grain boundary in a HEA will alleviate local strain concentrations and reduce the deleterious effects of rapid elemental segregation, thereby suppressing brittle intergranular fracture at high temperatures.
generation.material_initial_state: A precipitation-strengthened, single-phase high-entropy alloy (similar in composition to those processed by selective laser melting).
generation.intervention: Implement controlled slow cooling or post heat-treatment processing to transform straight grain boundaries into a serrated morphology without altering the overall phase constitution.
generation.conditions: Perform tensile and creep tests at elevated temperatures (around 650°C) that are known to induce GB embrittlement in straight-boundary samples.
generation.structural_mediator: Serrated grain boundary profiles that interrupt continuous paths for crack propagation and dissipate local stresses.
generation.mechanism: The undulating grain boundary morphology reduces local strain concentration and disrupts the continuity of segregation-induced weakening, thereby delaying or preventing the onset of brittle intergranular fracture.
generation.predicted_outcome: Samples with serrated grain boundaries will display significantly higher tensile fracture strains (e.g., >3.5 times improvement) and extended creep rupture lives (e.g., up to 400× longer) compared to samples with straight grain boundaries.
generation.baseline: Identical HEA composition processed with conventional cooling rates leading to straight grain boundaries.
generation.boundary: Applicable for high-temperature service conditions (∼650°C) under tensile and creep loads.
generation.uncertainty: The precise geometric parameters (amplitude and wavelength of the serration) required for optimal performance are not fully defined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of HEA samples with identical composition: one processed to yield serrated GB morphology via controlled cooling and one with straight GBs via rapid cooling. Test both sets under identical tensile and creep conditions at 650°C.
measurements: Microstructural analysis of GB morphology via SEM/TEM
Tensile and creep tests measuring ductility, fracture strain, and rupture life
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the samples with serrated grain boundaries do not exhibit statistically significant improvements in ductility and resistance to intergranular cracking compared to the straight-boundary samples, the hypothesis is falsified.

However, when testing temperature was increased to 650°C, a significant hot ductility drop was observed for HT-1 sample. According to Figure 7(b), the facet cleavage surface and the limited amount of plastic deformation indicate that the failure mechanism was brittle intergranular fracture. The brittleness of HT-1 sample was even more pronounced under creep at 650°C as the creep fracture strain was only 0.03%. Cleavage edges on crept fracture surface (Figure 9(b)) and crack propagation along straight grain boundary (Figure 10(b)) indicate the vulnerability of straight grain boundary in HT-1 samples at elevated temperature. According to the local strain concentration at triple junctions of grain boundaries (Figure 11(a)), it is probable that HT-1 samples encountered an embrittlement at 650°C. The initiation of creep damage of HT-1 sample was a result of vacancy coalescence on grain boundaries perpendicular to the loading direction and severe strain concentration at grain boundaries. papers.title: Deformation-induced grain boundary segregation in a powder-metallurgy ultrafine-grained MoNbTaTiV refractory high-entropy alloy.
papers.approach: Powder metallurgy, mechanical alloying, spark plasma sintering, and hot deformation experiments at varied temperatures and strain rates to monitor segregation behavior.
papers.findings: At relatively low deformation temperatures and high strain rates, component elemental segregation is observed near grain boundaries. As the deformation temperature increases and strain rate decreases, the segregation gradually disappears. The study links dislocation activity with the accumulation of certain elements (e.g., Ta, Mo) at grain boundaries.
papers.mechanism: Dislocation motion under plastic deformation causes atoms to migrate and accumulate at grain boundaries; the stored internal energy and increased vacancy formation further drive segregation. This segregation modulates local hardness and potentially GB cohesion.

papers.title: Grain boundary decohesion by nanoclustering Ni and Cr separately in CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloys.
papers.approach: Tensile testing at various temperatures combined with atom probe tomography and microscopic analysis to resolve nanosegregation at grain boundaries.
papers.findings: At intermediate temperatures (e.g., near 500°C), single-phase HEAs show ductility loss correlated with the nanosegregation of principal elements (Cr, Ni, and Mn) at grain boundaries that leads to intergranular cracking. In contrast, a dual-phase variant with preexisting Cr-rich sigma precipitates shows improved ductility due to migration of embrittling elements into these precipitates.
papers.mechanism: Fast nanosegregation of principal elements to grain boundaries reduces cohesion, promoting brittle intergranular fracture. Engineering a GB segregation strategy (using preexisting precipitates) can capture embrittling elements and mitigate ductility loss.

papers.title: Mitigating Strain Localization via Stabilized Phase Boundaries for Strengthening Multi-Principal Element Alloys.
papers.system: Multi-principal element alloys (MPEAs) with dual-phase (nanoscale BCC and FCC) architectures
papers.approach: Microstructural design inspired by enamel with stabilized phase boundaries aimed at facilitating trans‐phase dislocation migration, studied using mechanical testing and atomic-scale calculations.
papers.findings: The introduced dual-phase structures show enhanced tensile strength and ductility by alleviating strain localization. The mixed-phase boundaries distribute strain and enable continuous dislocation transfer, reducing the likelihood of intergranular crack initiation.
papers.mechanism: The stabilized phase boundaries act both as barriers and as channels enabling dislocation motion across adjacent phases, effectively mitigating the typical stress concentration at grain boundaries seen in single-phase materials.

papers.title: Effect of serrated grain boundary on tensile and creep properties of a precipitation strengthened high entropy alloy.
papers.system: A precipitation-strengthened high-entropy alloy processed by selective laser melting (composition including Al, Co, Cr, Ni, Ti, Nb, Zr, with trace B)
papers.approach: Heat treatment to modify grain boundary morphology from straight to serrated, combined with tensile and creep testing at high temperatures (around 650°C) and supporting molecular dynamics simulations.
papers.findings: Serrated grain boundaries yield significantly improved high-temperature ductility and creep rupture life (up to 3.5× and 400× improvements, respectively) compared to straight grain boundaries. The serrated morphology promotes more homogenous strain distribution and reduces local strain concentration, particularly at triple junctions.
papers.mechanism: The undulating (serrated) grain boundaries disrupt local strain localization and inhibit fast intergranular crack propagation, thereby enhancing resistance to brittle failure during high-temperature service.

papers.title: Microstructure and Mechanical Properties of Intergranular Boride Precipitation-Toughened HfMoNbTaTiZr Refractory High-Entropy Alloy.
papers.system: HfMoNbTaTiZr refractory high-entropy alloy with minor boron addition (RHEA-B)
papers.approach: Minor addition of boron to promote intergranular boride (likely (Hf, Zr)B2) precipitation; mechanical testing and microstructural characterization comparing alloys with and without boron.
papers.findings: The boron-added alloy exhibits intergranular boride precipitation that markedly increases grain boundary cohesion without altering the matrix hardness. This results in enhanced work hardenability and ductility, with a shift in failure mode from intergranular to predominantly transgranular fracture.
papers.mechanism: The formation of intergranular borides strengthens the grain boundary region by mitigating segregation-induced decohesion, compensating for element segregation that might otherwise lead to brittle behavior.

papers.title: Deformation Behaviors in Single BCC-Phase Refractory Multi-Principal Element Alloys under Dynamic Conditions.
papers.system: BCC-phase NbTaTiV refractory multi-principal element alloy (RMPEA)
papers.approach: Dynamic mechanical testing over a wide strain-rate window (10^−3 to 10^3 s^−1) and temperature range (room temperature to 850°C) combined with microstructural and density functional theory analysis.
papers.findings: Under high strain-rate conditions, the formation of thin twins is observed which enhance strain-hardening, though competing with adiabatic heating effects. The alloy shows modest strain-rate sensitivity and maintains mechanical stability up to high temperatures.
papers.mechanism: The interplay between dislocation activity, twinning, and subtle temperature effects (leading to adiabatic heating) establishes a dynamic equilibrium that governs mechanical response. Although not focused solely on GB segregation, the work emphasizes temperature and rate as critical in activation of deformation mechanisms.

established: Conventional alloys exhibit toughness loss due to grain-boundary segregation and brittle intergranular precipitation driven by trace elements.

High-entropy and multi-principal element alloys, despite suppressing deleterious intermetallic formation and grain coarsening, can also undergo elemental segregation at grain boundaries under certain conditions.
Temperature and strain rate critically affect the degree of segregation and thus the mechanical response, with lower temperatures and high strain rates favoring segregation.

approaches_tried.approach: GB segregation engineering via preexisting secondary phases (e.g., Cr-rich sigma phases) in CrMnFeCoNi HEAs
approaches_tried.outcome: Successfully mitigated ductility loss at intermediate temperatures by diverting fast-segregating embrittling elements from GBs; observed improvement in ductility.

approaches_tried.approach: Modifying grain boundary morphology (e.g., serrated GBs via reduced cooling rates) in precipitation-strengthened HEAs
approaches_tried.outcome: Significantly enhanced hot ductility and creep rupture life through more uniform strain distribution and reduced local strain concentration.

approaches_tried.approach: Addition of minor alloying elements (e.g., boron) to induce intergranular precipitation of borides
approaches_tried.outcome: Enhanced grain boundary cohesion, shifting failure from intergranular to transgranular modes and improving work hardenability and ductility.

mechanisms: Dislocation‐mediated atomic diffusion leading to rapid segregation of principal elements at grain boundaries.
Nanosegregation of elements such as Ni, Cr, and Mn at GBs that reduces interfacial cohesion and promotes intergranular cracking.
Modification of GB morphology (e.g., serration) to disperse strain concentration and retard cracking.
Precipitation of secondary phases (e.g., Cr-rich sigma, borides) that act as sinks for embrittling elements and enhance GB strength.
disagreements: The role of grain refinement is debated: some studies indicate finer grains promote segregation (by increasing total GB area), whereas others report that refined structures may improve ductility if segregation is mitigated by other means.

There is a divergence in understanding how much of the loss of toughness is due solely to segregation in single-phase HEAs versus contributions from secondary phase precipitation, with some studies emphasizing segregation even without visible precipitates.
open_questions: What is the critical threshold of principal element segregation in a single-phase HEA that triggers brittle behavior?
How do service conditions (temperature, strain rate, and loading mode) interact with segregation kinetics in pristine single-phase high-entropy alloys?
What is the interplay between dislocation dynamics/twinning and grain boundary segregation in governing the transition from ductile to brittle failure in these systems?
opportunities: Perform a controlled comparative study between an initially single-phase HEA and a compositionally similar dual-phase alloy (with preexisting secondary phases) to directly assess the impact of fast principal element segregation on GB cohesion.
Systematically vary deformation temperature and strain rate to map the segregation kinetics and correlate them to toughness degradation in single-phase HEAs.

Combine grain boundary morphology modification (e.g., through tailored cooling rates to induce serration) with controlled compositional tuning to minimize segregation while maintaining high-temperature stability.

Utilize in situ microstructural characterization (e.g., atom probe tomography and in situ TEM) during deformation to decouple dislocation-induced segregation from thermally activated diffusion processes in service-relevant conditions.

directions.direction: Control of deformation conditions to trigger dislocation‐induced grain boundary segregation
directions.assessment: Directly addresses the emergence of brittle behavior by linking high strain rate/low temperature deformation to rapid elemental segregation at grain boundaries. Physics and prior APT/TEM studies support that dislocation activity can drive segregation; however, the precise threshold remains uncertain. It is experimentally feasible by comparing different strain‐rate and temperature regimes.

directions.direction: Engineering of preexisting secondary precipitates for solute sequestration at grain boundaries
directions.assessment: By comparing a single‐phase HEA with a dual‐phase microstructure (containing Cr‐rich precipitates), this approach tests whether pre‐existing precipitates can capture the rapidly segregating embrittling elements. The established evidence in HEAs supports a segregation engineering strategy, and the comparison is feasible through controlled heat treatment.

directions.direction: Modification of grain boundary morphology (e.g., serration versus straight boundaries)
directions.assessment: Altering GB morphology to produce serrated rather than planar boundaries is known to reduce local strain concentration and possibly the deleterious effects of segregation. This approach leverages prior evidence from precipitation‐strengthened alloys and is directly comparable to conventional alloy behavior where straight GBs typically embrittle.

directions.direction: Systematic evaluation of strain‐rate effects (dynamic versus quasi‐static loading) in single‐phase HEAs
directions.assessment: Testing under different strain rates can isolate the interplay between adiabatic heating, dislocation dynamics, and segregation kinetics. While conventional alloys are known to soften or embrittle under certain dynamic conditions, the unique behavior of HEAs under extreme strain rates is less explored, providing a direct test of the hypothesis.

directions.direction: In situ atomistic and microstructural characterization during deformation
directions.assessment: Using in situ APT, TEM, or even molecular dynamics simulation to directly map the onset of segregation and its spatial correlation with crack initiation could decouple the relative roles of dynamic dislocation activity versus thermally activated diffusion. Although promising, the experimental complexity is higher.

candidates.hypothesis: Under high strain rate deformation (≥10^3 s⁻¹) of an ultrafine-grained MoNbTaTiV refractory HEA, if external cooling maintains near-isothermal conditions to suppress adiabatic heating, rapid dislocation motion will nonetheless drive accelerated grain boundary segregation of key elements (e.g., Ta and Mo) before dynamic recrystallization can homogenize the microstructure, leading to brittle intergranular failure. In contrast, quasi‐static loading (≈10⁻³ s⁻¹) allows sufficient time for diffusion and recrystallization, preserving ductility.
candidates.intervention: Subject samples to tensile tests under controlled high strain rate (≥10^3 s⁻¹) and quasi‐static (≈10⁻³ s⁻¹) conditions while employing an external cooling system to hold the temperature constant.
candidates.changes: Decoupled the contributions of adiabatic heating from segregation kinetics by explicitly mandating isothermal conditions and external cooling to maintain constant temperature during high strain rate tests. candidates.hypothesis: By engineering a serrated (undulated) grain boundary morphology with defined geometric parameters (target amplitude of 0.5–1 µm and wavelength of 2–5 µm) in a precipitation-strengthened HEA, local strain concentrations and continuous segregation pathways are interrupted, effectively reducing intergranular brittle fracture at elevated temperatures.
candidates.intervention: Implement controlled slow cooling or tailored post heat-treatment to transform conventional straight grain boundaries into serrated morphologies with the target amplitude and wavelength.
candidates.changes: Added quantitative parameters for the serrated grain boundary geometry and emphasized that the intervention targets the mitigation of local strain concentration as well as disruption to segregation continuity. Minor clarifications were made regarding the single-phase nature complemented by minor precipitates.

candidates.hypothesis: In a single‐phase equiatomic CrMnFeCoNi HEA, uniaxial tensile deformation at an intermediate temperature (~500°C) under high strain rates (10–10² s⁻¹) promotes rapid dislocation motion that selectively drives nanosegregation of Ni, Cr, and Mn toward grain boundaries. This localized segregation reduces GB cohesion, leading to a switch from ductile transgranular to brittle intergranular fracture.
candidates.intervention: Subject samples to tensile deformation at 500°C under two distinct strain rate regimes: a high strain rate (10–10² s⁻¹) versus a quasi‐static rate (≈10⁻³ s⁻¹).
candidates.changes: Clarified why Ni, Cr, and Mn are the primary elements expected to segregate based on their lower effective diffusion barriers and their known propensity from previous APT studies. Also tightened strain rate and temperature ranges for clearer testing conditions.

candidates.hypothesis: Introducing preexisting Cr-rich σ-phase precipitates selectively along the grain boundaries of a single-phase CrMnFeCoNi HEA sequesters fast-segregating embrittling elements (Ni, Cr, Mn), thereby preserving GB cohesion and maintaining ductility at intermediate temperatures (600–700°C) by preventing brittle intergranular failure.
candidates.intervention: Apply a tailored heat treatment (with precisely controlled temperature and duration) to induce controlled precipitation of Cr-rich σ-phases along GBs without disrupting the single-phase matrix.
candidates.changes: Expanded the discussion to address potential trade-offs (e.g., low-temperature ductility) and clarified that controlled heat treatment parameters (e.g., time and temperature) must be optimized to yield a desired volume fraction and morphology of Cr-rich precipitates. Emphasized that precipitates act as sinks for embrittling elements.
